title: Cloudflare’s OHTTP Gateway Refuses to Decrypt Requests That Arrive Through Cloudflare
gist: Cloudflare opened a closed beta of an OHTTP Gateway that deliberately refuses to decrypt requests relayed through Cloudflare itself, enforcing the non-collusion premise of RFC 9458. Hacker News reaction centered on adoption, relay trust, lack of forward secrecy and lost WAF metadata rather than the cryptography.

themes.theme: OHTTP privacy architecture and Cloudflare's refusal rule

insights.claim: Oblivious HTTP (RFC 9458) splits a request between a relay that sees the client IP but not content and a gateway that sees content but only the relay's address, so privacy holds only if two different operators run the hops.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Privacy products built on this protocol are only as strong as the separation of operators; watch who controls both hops.

insights.claim: Cloudflare's OHTTP Gateway will not decrypt requests arriving from Cloudflare Workers or Cloudflare-proxied hosts, because that would put the client-identifying hop and the decryption hop under one company.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A vendor encoding a trust constraint into the product is a differentiator versus privacy claims based on policy alone.
insights.quote: the Gateway will not decrypt requests that reach it from Cloudflare Workers or from hosts proxied through Cloudflare
insights.locator: The design decision that drew most of the attention

insights.claim: Cloudflare is not supplying a relay for the Gateway and is renaming its existing Privacy Gateway to Cloudflare OHTTP Relay; the hard part for customers is credibly promising users they will not inspect client-identifying logs, not running the relay.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The real cost and friction of adoption sits with the customer's operational trust, which may slow uptake.
insights.quote: verifiably promise to your users that you won’t inspect logs with client identifiers

insights.claim: OHTTP protects only at the network layer: if an app puts a session token, email or username in the sealed request body, the gateway operator regains the identity the protocol was meant to hide.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Privacy-by-transport claims from app vendors need scrutiny of what the payload contains.
insights.quote: it’s up to you not to send identifying information
insights.locator: Protection stops at the network layer

insights.claim: The Gateway binds to a zone at a fixed /.well-known/ohttp-gateway path, Cloudflare manages the HPKE keys, supports standard and chunked OHTTP (chunked recommended), and runs Cloudflare Access before decryption so the relay can be authenticated.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Shows the product is a managed, zone-bound add-on that integrates with Cloudflare's existing security stack.
insights.locator: The Gateway itself binds to a zone

insights.claim: Cloudflare cites Flo Health's Anonymous Mode and Apple's Private Cloud Compute as production OHTTP deployments, and its Reference Image work with Apple uses the same transport to request timestamps without revealing the requester.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: OHTTP is gaining traction in privacy-sensitive consumer and AI-inference products tied to Apple's ecosystem.

insights.claim: The Gateway launches this fall as a paid add-on to a customer's zone, with the self-serve closed beta starting now and no price published.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Another monetized privacy add-on for Cloudflare; pricing is the unknown to monitor.
insights.locator: Cloudflare says the Gateway launches this fall

insights.claim: A Hacker News commenter argued that charging for a privacy add-on is a poor incentive if the goal is to improve privacy generally.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Signals community pushback on monetization of privacy infrastructure.

insights.claim: OHTTP suits narrow stateless-request use cases where the gateway must not correlate multiple requests from one client; compared to a SOCKS5 proxy it avoids a new TCP connection per request, allows TLS resumption and long-lived relay connections, a latency win for workloads like DNS over HTTPS.
insights.speaker: Hacker News commenter gsnedders (reported by Steef-Jan Wiggers)
insights.so_what: Defines where OHTTP is the right tool and where it is not.
insights.locator: Commenter gsnedders gave the most detailed comparison

insights.claim: OHTTP has no forward secrecy: disclosure of the gateway key lets the relay decrypt recorded traffic that used that key, while disclosure of client-relay or relay-gateway keys matters much less.
insights.speaker: Hacker News commenter gsnedders (reported by Steef-Jan Wiggers)
insights.so_what: Key custody at the gateway is the critical risk point for deployments.
insights.quote: disclosure of the gateway key essentially means the relay can decrypt recorded traffic
insights.locator: He also named what the design gives up

insights.claim: Open operational questions after the announcement include whether Cloudflare's TLS-fingerprint-based WAF still works under OHTTP and how IP-based banning survives, since client metadata is hidden from the origin.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Unresolved abuse-handling tradeoffs could limit enterprise adoption.

insights.claim: A self-hosted relay run for only a handful of people defeats its own purpose, because the service then knows any request through it came from that small group.
insights.speaker: Hacker News commenter palata (reported by Steef-Jan Wiggers)
insights.so_what: Anonymity-set size drives the value of relay deployments.

insights.claim: The discussion suggests teams will argue about client availability, relay value and lost Cloudflare-side metadata rather than the cryptography, and a key adoption question is whether any current proxy, tunnel or VPN software supports OHTTP as a transport.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Client-side ecosystem support is the gating factor for OHTTP growth.

insights.claim: OHTTP is not general browsing privacy like Tor ('a two-hop Tor circuit with a predetermined gateway'); it fits app vendors wanting telemetry, inference or lookups without tying requests to users, and a centralized provider serving much of the internet still aggregates which IP visited which site.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Clarifies the addressable market: app-embedded privacy rather than consumer VPN-style demand.
insights.locator: The closest comparison in the thread was Tor
